newsitem.title: USA: U.S. has not found Dhahran bombers, Perry says.
newsitem.headline: U.S. has not found Dhahran bombers, Perry says.

text.p: The United States has not found a culprit for the bombing that killed 19 U.S. airmen in Saudi Arabia, Defense Secretary William Perry said on Friday, responding to a report that Saudi authorities had arrested 40 people.
Asked about The Washington Post report, which also said Saudi Arabia was pinning partial blame on Iran, Perry told reporters: "We have reached no conclusions about who was responsible for this."
He would not confirm or deny the report, saying only that he had pressed Saudi authorities for cooperation.

Two independent sources with knowledge of the investigation said they believed the report to be essentially correct. "The arrests have been made, it's common knowledge," said one source who declined to be further identified.
The Saudi Arabian embassy in Washington declined comment. "The investigation is ongoing. We can't comment on it. At the appropriate time, the appropriate people will comment," a spokesman said.

Echoing comments from top Pentagon officials since the June 25 truck bomb attack on a military housing complex in Dhahran, Perry said Saudi authorities and the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation were still conducting the probe.

"This investigation is still under way and I cannot comment on the status of this or any other investigation still being conducted," he said at a news conference with South Korean Defense Minister Kim Dong-jin.
An FBI spokesman declined to comment on the report, except to say the investigation continued. But other FBI officials privately expressed frustration at what they called a lack of Saudi cooperation.
The FBI has three agents in Saudi Arabia investigating the bombing, but was considering pulling them out without replacing them in a "symbolic message" of displeasure, one official said.

Although FBI chief Louis Freeh went to Saudi Arabia twice this summer and won pledges of cooperation, the officials said the agents have not been allowed to sit in on interrogations and had not been told about any arrests.

Quoting unnamed sources close to the investigation, the Post said on Friday that Saudi security officials were holding some 40 Saudi citizens for alleged involvement in the attack. The report said Saudi Arabia was convinced the attack was part of a broad conspiracy backed by Iran.
The suspects, who have been secretly imprisoned for at least three months, included a man who Saudi officials claim was the driver of the explosive-laden vehicle, the Post said.

Media reports have said the United States was not satisfied with Saudi cooperation in investigating the bombing and another attack on last Nov. 13 that killed five Americans and two Indians in Riyadh.

Asked if he was satisfied with Saudi Arabia's cooperation, Perry said: "In my discussions with the senior Saudi officials I have made very clear the importance to our defense departments of full cooperation in this investigation. They have promised us at the highest levels of the Saudi government full cooperation. Any further comments on that would have to come from the FBI."

The newspaper said the internal inquiry was complete and what remained of the Saudi probe was being conducted outside of the kingdom. It said the Saudi government had obtained confessions from some of those arrested and other evidence implicating Iran as the instigator and sponsor of the attack.
In addition, the Post said, there was evidence suggesting potential advance knowledge or involvement by Syria.

The newspaper said Saudi security officials had not yet fully briefed Washington on their findings, partly out of concern that the Clinton administration, in the days before the election, might rush to retaliate in a way that the Saudis would view as harmful.
Saudi officials had privately notified senior U.S. officials that they wanted to take part in any decision on how to respond to the evidence, the Post added.
